content_metadata.description: An informative video explaining the significance of Makar Sankranti in Indian culture, its astronomical basis, and the historical context of its date shift.

qAndA.answer: It is based on the sun's motion, while most other Hindu festivals are based on the moon's motion.
qAndA.question: What is unique about the Makar Sankranti festival compared to other Hindu festivals?

qAndA.answer: The Earth's equator is tilted to the ecliptic plane by 23.5 degrees. This tilt affects the amount of sunlight different regions receive throughout the year.
qAndA.question: What causes the four seasons on Earth?

qAndA.answer: December 21st, which coincided with Makar Sankranti and the winter solstice.
qAndA.question: What date historically marked the beginning of winter in India?

qAndA.answer: The Gregorian calendar does not perfectly align with the Earth's actual revolution period, causing a gradual shift in the date of Sankranti.
qAndA.question: Why does Makar Sankranti no longer fall on December 21st?

qAndA.answer: It is celebrated on the next day.
qAndA.question: When is Makar Sankranti celebrated if the sun enters Capricornus after sunset?

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator introduces Makar Sankranti as a unique Indian festival based on the sun's motion.
The meaning of 'Makar Sankranti' is explained as the sun's transition into Capricornus.
The narrator highlights the uniqueness of Makar Sankranti as a solar-based festival amidst lunar-based Hindu festivals.
It is explained that there are twelve Sankrantis in a year, marking the sun's entry into each zodiac sign.
The narrator describes Earth's revolution around the sun and its tilted equator causing seasons.
The Earth's position on December 21st and its impact on seasons in the Northern and Southern hemispheres are explained.
The narrator states that Makar Sankranti historically coincided with the winter solstice.
The significance of Makar Sankranti for agriculture is discussed.
The observation that Makar Sankranti no longer falls on December 21st is addressed.
The shift in Makar Sankranti's date to January 14th or 15th is highlighted.
The reason for the date shift is explored through data from 2001 to 2008.
The conclusion is drawn that Makar Sankranti is celebrated the day after the sun enters Capricornus if the transition happens after sunset.
The Gregorian calendar system and its impact on Makar Sankranti's date are introduced.
The narrator explains how the leap year system in the Gregorian calendar addresses the time surplus.
A graph visually illustrates the forward shift of Sankranti over time.
The narrator predicts the future shift in Sankranti's date to January 15th.
Despite the date shift, Makar Sankranti remains a significant festival in India.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: India has a plethora of festivals and we all enjoy celebrating this festival to the fullest.
It is a part of India's cultural tradition for thousands of years.
But have you ever tried to understand the meaning behind these festivals?
Could our festivals be indicative of something much deeper than just celebration?
In the next few minutes we are going to discuss the meaning of one such festival of India
called as the Makarsankranti.
Makarsankranti is a unique festival out of all the other festivals of Biharad.
The reason for this uniqueness is that it is a festival based on the motion of the
sun while all the other Hindu festivals are based on the motion of the moon.
The term Makarsankranti is a combination of two words.
Makarabh which is the Indian astronomical name for Capricornis and Sankranti which comes
from the word Sankraman and it means transition.
So Makarsankranti means the transition of sun into Capricornis.
That are a total of 12 Sankrantis in a year.
Every time the sun enters a new rashi a Sankranti is said to have occurred.
So why is the Makarsankranti given so much importance?
We all know that the earth revolves around the sun in an elliptical orbit and the earth's
equator is tilted to the ecliptic plane by 23.5 degrees.
This tilt is the cause for the four types of seasons on planet earth namely winter,
spring, summer and autumn.
On 21st of December the earth is positioned in space in such a way that it is northern hemisphere
is tilted away from the sun by 23.5 degrees while the southern hemisphere is tilted towards
the sun by 23.5 degrees.
Because of this orientation the northern hemisphere receives lesser amount of heat and sunlight
as compared to the southern hemisphere because the sun stays low in the sky in the northern
hemisphere.
This signifies the start of winter season in the north and the summer season in the
south and this position of the earth occurs on 21st of December since all of India lies
in the northern hemisphere of the earth.
The date of 21st of December marks the beginning of winter season even in India.
So how does it explain the importance of Makarsankranti?
The reason is in the ancient past the sun's entry into Capricornus occurred on the day
of winter solstice and it means that the Makarsankranta used to coincide with the winter solstice.
Thus in ancient India the festival of Makarsankranti marked the onset of winter season and hence it
was considered to be of vital importance especially for agriculture.
Since Makarsankranti signified the start of winter season this was the reason for the
traditions like consuming sessay when jaggery products in your meals or wearing black colored
clothes starting from this day onwards so that your body could muster enough heat to keep
you warm during the winter season.
Another important aspect of the Makarsankranti occurring on the day of winter solstice in the
past was that on this day the sun was seen in its southernmost position in the sky.
From this day onwards the sun begins its journey towards the north which is called Uttarayan
in Indian astronomer.
Thus Makarsankranti not only marked the beginning of the winter season but also the start of Uttarayan.
But today we see that Makarsankranti no longer falls on 21st of December the winter solstice
day but its date has now shifted to 14th and sometimes it occurs even on 15th of January.
So what might be the reason behind this forward shift in the date of Makarsankranti?
Let's try to understand these reasons analytically.
If we see the date on which Makarsankranti occurred between 2001 to 2008 we find that Makarsankranti
occurred on 15th of January in 2004 and in 2008 but it is celebrated on 14th of January
in the rest of the years between 2001 and 2008.
So what exactly is happening?
The answer to this riddle lies in the time at which the sun enters Capricorn's.
If we see the time of the sun's transition into Capricorn's for the years 2001 to 2008
we see that in 2004 the sun entered Capricorn's at 1143 pm that is after the sunset of 14th
of January.
Same thing happened in 2008 when the sun entered Capricorn's at 1207 am which is again
after the sunset of 14th of January and is the Makarsankranti was celebrated on the next
day that is on 15th of January.
This brings to us an important assertion that if the sun enters Capricorn's after the
sunset then the Makarsankranti is celebrated on the next day.
But the second reason for this forward shift of the date of Makarsankranti is due to the
Gregorian or English calendar system.
The Gregorian calendar measures 365 days in a year but the earth takes a tad bit longer
than 365 days to complete one revolution.
Considering a side area earlier the earth takes 365 days 6 hours and 9 minutes to complete
one revolution.
This surplus of 6 hours and 9 minutes is not counted in the Gregorian calendar.
After 4 years this surplus gets accumulated to 24 hours and 36 minutes which means at the
end of the 4 years the Gregorian calendar ends about 24 hours earlier than the actual revolution
period of the earth.
Fortunately Gregorian calendar has a provision of rectifying this error by the addition of
the liberty after every 4 years.
So the error of 24 hours no longer persists.
But the surplus of 36 minutes is still unaccounted and this surplus of 36 minutes after every 4
years also shifts forward the time of Makarsankranti by 36 minutes every 4 years.
To understand it better let's take a look at the graph of the time of Makarsankranti
The forward shift of Sankranti is easily noticeable.
So can we calculate the number of years after which Sankranti will be shifted to 15th of
January for 3 consecutive years.
The 4 year shift pattern of Sankranti's day of 14, 14, 14 and 15 changed to 14, 14,
In this period the sun's entry into Capricornus in 2010 was at 1230pm.
Hence for this pattern to change again this entry should move forward till 619pm that
is by about 6 hours or 360 minutes.
As we learned earlier if Sankranti shifts forward by 36 minutes every 4 years then it will
shift forward by 360 minutes after 40 years.
So the pattern will change to 14, 15, 15, 15 during 20, 49 to 20, 52.
Following the same cycle few decades later Makarsankranti will be permanently shifted to 15th
of January and it will keep on shifting forward by 1 day every 40 years.
Nonetheless Makarsankranti is still celebrated in India with the same gusto and joy and
it is still considered as one of the most important festivals of India.

youtube_description:
14th January is probably one of the biggest days for people living in the Northern Indian Side. Yes, we are talking about Makar Sankranti, which marks the beginning of the joyous spring season, marking the end of Winter, and also the starting of the Rabi Crop plantation. One can find the skies full of kites, a way people like to celebrate this day.

While we are aware about the festival, we would also like to enlighten the fact that this day is also important astronomically. How? well, Makar Sankranti can be loosely translated as “Transition of Sun in Capriconous”, Makar being Capricon, and Sankranti being a form of Sankraman, which means transition. In fact there are 12 Sankrantis in India, one for each Zodiac! 

But why only Makar Sankranti is only given importance and not the other 11 ? How does Makar Sankranti become so important to understand from a Mathematical and Astronomical point of view ? Stay tuned to understand more !
